LESSON 103 OF 106·Cyber Security in the Real World

Careers and Specialisations (and What to Learn Next)

What security roles actually involve, why job titles are the unreliable part, and how to choose a direction without a salary chart or a promise.

Applied Foundation13 min
Why this matters

Security is not one job. It splits into technical specialisms, into defensive and offensive work, and into the part of the job that is deciding what to do about it. Knowing which of those you are is more useful than a list of job titles.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • The main technical families are security operations, security engineering, application security, and governance and risk.
  • Offensive work exists as a legitimate career, but the entry routes and the required judgement are different from defensive work.
  • Most roles are a mixture of technical and non-technical, and the non-technical half is what determines whether the technical half gets used.
  • The specialisms are converging: cloud, identity and supply chain have blurred the boundaries between them.
  • Portability comes from fundamentals and from a verifiable way of demonstrating you have them.

The background

  • The profession grew out of system administration and network engineering, and that grounding still shows.
  • Consulting and audit created a separate non-technical track that never had a technical equivalent.
  • Cloud platforms moved the centre of gravity from the data centre to the identity provider.
  • Current hiring increasingly asks for demonstrable hands-on work, and less for credentials alone.

Real-world examples

  • A generalist who can read code, configure a platform and write a policy is more employable than a narrow specialist in one of them.
  • A technical finding nobody communicates does not change anything, and that is the most common reason good security work is undervalued.
  • Someone who only has certification knowledge struggles once the environment does not match the exam.

What to look for

  • Check whether the role involves the work you would rather do, since titles vary and descriptions often do not.
  • Check whether you would be expected to communicate with non-technical stakeholders, because most roles are.
  • Check whether the team actually has the authority to fix what it finds.
  • Check whether the role has a path, or whether it is the same job with more years.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Learn the fundamentals properly: operating systems, networking, and how identity actually works.
  • Demonstrate capability with something you built, broke and explained, rather than with a list of credentials.
  • Practise writing: a clear finding or a short design note is a genuine differentiator.
  • Get comfortable with the business language, since you will need to prioritise in those terms.
  • Pick a specialism deliberately after a broad base, rather than specialising before you know what the work involves.
